paragraphs.title: God's Warning Against Idolatry and the Pronouncement of Punishment

easy.explanation: Jeremiah spoke to all the Jews dwelling in the land of Egypt.
easy.q: To whom did Jeremiah speak the word of the Lord?

easy.explanation: The cities were described as a desolation with no man dwelling in them.
easy.q: What was the condition of Jerusalem and the cities of Judah?

easy.explanation: They burned incense and served other gods.
easy.q: What did the Jews do that provoked the Lord to anger?

answers: Their wickedness and service to other gods
medium.explanation: The destruction followed their wickedness, idolatry, and disobedience.
medium.q: According to Jeremiah, what caused the destruction of Judah's cities?

answers: To warn the people not to do the abominable thing
To command them to move to Egypt
medium.explanation: The prophets warned them to stop worshiping other gods.
medium.q: Why did the Lord repeatedly send His prophets?

answers: Almost no survivors would be left
Everyone would remain in the land
medium.explanation: The phrase describes nearly complete destruction.
medium.q: What does the phrase “to leave you none to remain” mean?

answers: The Lord's warnings versus the people's conduct
challenge.explanation: The Lord warned them through the prophets, but they continued in their sin.
challenge.q: What central contrast appears at the beginning of the passage?

answers: Serving other gods led to destruction and ruin
Serving other gods saved the cities
Serving other gods caused the people to return to Judah
challenge.explanation: Idolatry is presented as the cause of the destruction and judgment.
challenge.q: What connection does the passage make between idolatry and punishment?

answers: To show that the people had already won
To give an example of the result of the same behavior
To prove that Egypt was safe
challenge.explanation: The ruined cities of Judah demonstrate the consequences of sin.
challenge.q: Why does Jeremiah mention the destruction that had already happened?

paragraphs.title: The People's Refusal and Their Defense of the Queen of Heaven

answers: The men, women, and all the people
easy.explanation: The passage describes men, women, and all the people answering him.
They said to Jeremiah, “We will not hearken unto thee.”
easy.q: To whom did the people say they would not hearken?

easy.explanation: They declared that they would continue worshiping the queen of heaven.
easy.q: To whom did they say they would burn incense and pour out drink offerings?

answers: They had plenty of food and were well
medium.explanation: They claimed, “Then had we plenty of victuals, and were well, and saw no evil.”
medium.q: What did the people claim happened when they worshiped the queen of heaven?

answers: They lacked everything and were consumed by sword and famine
medium.explanation: They associated stopping the worship with want, sword, and famine.
medium.q: What did they claim happened after they stopped the worship?

answers: Liquid offerings poured out in worship
medium.explanation: A drink offering was a liquid poured out as part of a ritual.
medium.q: In this passage, what are “drink offerings”?

answers: Their interpretation of their past experience
challenge.explanation: They claimed that their former prosperity resulted from the worship.
challenge.q: What is the basis of the people's argument for continuing the worship?

answers: They rejected his words and announced that they would continue
They asked him for a sign
challenge.explanation: They plainly refused to hearken to Jeremiah and insisted on continuing.
challenge.q: What does the people's answer reveal about their response to the prophet?

answers: The men and women expressed a united position
challenge.explanation: The response came from a gathering of men and women who shared the stated position.
challenge.q: How are the men and women portrayed in the people's response?

paragraphs.title: Jeremiah's Answer: Sin Caused the Destruction

answers: The people who had answered him
easy.explanation: Jeremiah answered all the people, including the women who had spoken.

answers: The names of the kings of Egypt
easy.explanation: Jeremiah said that the Lord remembered the incense they had burned.
easy.q: What did Jeremiah say the Lord remembered?

easy.explanation: The land became a desolation and an astonishment, without an inhabitant.
easy.q: What happened to the land because of the people's actions?

answers: Because of the evil of their doings and their abominations
Because they had not built a temple
medium.explanation: The stated reasons were the evil of their doings and the abominations they committed.
medium.q: Why could the Lord no longer bear their actions?

answers: Their sin and disobedience brought the evil upon them
There was no connection between their actions and the result
medium.explanation: The evil happened because they sinned and did not obey the Lord's voice.
medium.q: What relationship does Jeremiah show between sin and the evil that came upon the people?
In the phrase “the evil of your doings,” what does “doings” mean?

answers: He points to the desolation as evidence of the true result of their actions
He agrees that the worship helped them
He claims that Egypt never existed
challenge.explanation: Jeremiah points to the ruined land and the evil that came upon them.
challenge.q: How does Jeremiah refute the people's claim that the worship brought them prosperity?

answers: The people, their fathers, kings, and princes all burned incense
Only the kings of Egypt served other gods
challenge.explanation: Jeremiah refers to the people, their fathers, kings, and princes.
challenge.q: What detail connects the people's generation with earlier generations?

answers: The desolation was a real condition visible at that time
The desolation would occur only in the distant future
challenge.explanation: The phrase emphasizes that the land was actually desolate when Jeremiah spoke.
challenge.q: What does “as at this day” emphasize in the description of the land?

paragraphs.title: God's Oath to End the Worship and Bring Destruction

answers: All Judah dwelling in the land of Egypt
easy.explanation: He called all Judah in the land of Egypt to hear the word of the Lord.
easy.q: Whom did Jeremiah call to hear?

answers: Fulfill their vows to the queen of heaven
easy.explanation: They declared that they would fulfill their vows to burn incense and pour out drink offerings.
easy.q: What did the women and men declare they would do?

answers: To watch over them for good
To watch over them for evil
To bring them all back to Egypt
easy.explanation: The Lord said, “I will watch over them for evil, and not for good.”
easy.q: What did the Lord swear concerning the Jews in Egypt?

answers: They only spoke and did nothing
They spoke with their mouths and fulfilled their vows with their hands
medium.explanation: They said they would fulfill their vows and carried them out in action.
medium.q: What does the people's statement reveal about the connection between words and actions?

answers: The men of Judah in Egypt would be consumed by sword and famine
The worship would bring new prosperity
medium.explanation: The Lord declared that they would be consumed by the sword and famine.
medium.q: What would be the result of the Lord's oath?

medium.explanation: “To cut off” means to destroy, eliminate, or bring to an end.
medium.q: In this context, what does “to cut off” mean?

answers: To show that responsibility for the worship was shared
To excuse the men from responsibility
To say that only the women sinned
challenge.explanation: The worship is presented as a shared commitment of women and men.
challenge.q: Why does the passage emphasize that both women and men made and fulfilled the vows?

answers: The people promised to continue, while the Lord swore to bring destruction
The people asked forgiveness, while the Lord promised prosperity
The people left Egypt, while the Lord prevented their departure
challenge.explanation: The people insisted on their vows, but the Lord announced judgment.
challenge.q: What contrast appears between the people's declaration and the Lord's response?

answers: His watchfulness would be for judgment, not rescue
The Lord would not know what would happen
The people would receive only partial blessing
challenge.explanation: The phrase means that the Lord would watch over them in order to bring harm rather than deliverance.
challenge.q: What does “not for good” mean in the Lord's statement?

paragraphs.title: The Sign: A Few Refugees Will Return to Judah

answers: A small number who escaped the sword
easy.explanation: Only a small number that escaped the sword would return.
easy.q: Who would return from Egypt to the land of Judah?

answers: How many cities were in Egypt
easy.explanation: They would know whether the Lord's words or the people's words would stand.
easy.q: What would the remnant of Judah know because of the return?

answers: To show that the Lord's words would come true against them
easy.explanation: The sign would confirm that the Lord's words of judgment would stand.

answers: That the people were right to refuse
That the word of the Lord had come to pass
That Egypt had defeated its enemies
medium.explanation: The returning survivors would demonstrate that the Lord's word had been fulfilled.
medium.q: What would the return of the few refugees prove?

answers: A few people who could be counted
People who did not know how to count
medium.explanation: The phrase refers to a small and limited number of survivors.
medium.q: What does “a small number” mean in this passage?

answers: The refugees are only a very small part
medium.explanation: Only a small remnant would survive from among the Jews in Egypt.
medium.q: What is the relationship between the refugees and all the Jews in Egypt?

answers: It would be visible proof that the Lord's word had come to pass
It would cancel the whole punishment
It would show that Egypt was the chosen land
challenge.explanation: Their limited return would serve as concrete evidence that the Lord's judgment was fulfilled.
challenge.q: Why is the return of the few refugees called a “sign”?

answers: Whether the Lord's word or the people's claim was right
challenge.explanation: The passage contrasts the Lord's words with the words of the people.
challenge.q: What future dispute would the return of the refugees settle?

answers: The punishment would be severe and most of the people would not survive
The whole people would be saved
All the Jews of Egypt would return immediately
challenge.explanation: The small number of returnees shows the severity of the judgment.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the fact that only a few would return to Judah?

easy.explanation: The verse calls him Pharaohhophra, king of Egypt.

answers: Into the hand of his enemies and those who sought his life
Into the hand of the Jews in Egypt
easy.explanation: The Lord said He would give him into the hand of his enemies and those seeking his life.
easy.q: Into whose hand would Pharaohhophra be delivered?

easy.explanation: His fate was compared with that of Zedekiah, king of Judah.
easy.q: Whose fate was compared with Pharaohhophra's fate?

medium.explanation: Zedekiah was given into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar, king of Babylon.
medium.q: Into whose hand was Zedekiah given?

answers: Both were delivered into the hands of their enemies
medium.explanation: Both kings were handed over to enemies and those seeking their lives.
medium.q: What did Pharaohhophra's fate and Zedekiah's fate have in common?

answers: People seeking to harm or kill him
People seeking to learn from him
medium.explanation: The phrase refers to enemies who wanted to harm or kill him.
medium.q: What does “them that seek his life” mean?

answers: It shows that Egypt and its king were not a safe refuge
It proves that Egypt would save the Jews
challenge.explanation: The king's downfall shows that Egypt could not provide secure protection.
challenge.q: Why is it significant that Pharaohhophra, the king to whom the Jews fled, was also delivered to his enemies?

answers: Both were delivered into the hands of enemies, though they were different kings
challenge.explanation: The verse compares Pharaohhophra's being handed over with Zedekiah's similar fate.
challenge.q: What connection does the verse make between the king of Egypt and the king of Judah?

answers: Political power cannot prevent the fulfillment of the Lord's judgment
The kings of Egypt would protect Judah
challenge.explanation: The comparison shows that kings and political power remain subject to the Lord's decree.
challenge.q: What does the comparison with Zedekiah emphasize in the chapter's message?
